claims.claim: When someone you know is doing wrong, it is your duty to confront them about it.

stances.original: Nec ideo tamen ab huius modi culpa penitus alienus est, qui, licet praepositus non sit, in eis tamen, quibus uitae huius necessitate coniungitur, multa monenda uel arguenda nouit et neglegit, deuitans eorum offensiones (text at thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/civ1.shtml)
stances.summary: Correcting a person who is doing wrong is a duty of love, and not only for clergy. Staying quiet to avoid giving offence, or to keep a friendship, is itself a sin.
stances.quote: Nor is that man guiltless of the sin we speak of, who, though he be not a watchman, yet sees in the conduct of those with whom the relationships of this life bring him into contact, many things that should be blamed, and yet overlooks them, fearing to give offense
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF 1st series vol. 2, 1887
stances.context: Written c. 413. Augustine is explaining why good Christians suffered with the wicked in the sack of Rome: they had kept quiet about wrongs they saw "either because we shrink from the labor or are ashamed to offend them, or because we fear to lose good friendships". He adds a real qualification in the same chapter: holding back "because he seeks a more seasonable opportunity, or because he fears they may be made worse by his rebuke" is "a charitable consideration", not a sin. He says the same thing often and bluntly. Sermon 82 (Benedictine numbering; NPNF Sermon 32 on the New Testament, section 7, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/160332.htm, R.G. MacMullen 1888): "If you shall neglect this, you are worse than he... You are worse in keeping silence, than he in his reviling." The same sermon says to rebuke privately first, "sparing his shame", and to rebuke publicly only sins done in public (sections 7-10). The Rule, in its form for women (Letter 211.11, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102211.htm, J.G. Cunningham 1887): "you are not guiltless if by keeping silence you allow sisters to perish, whom you may correct by giving information of their faults" (Latin Rule, thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/reg.shtml: "Magis quippe innocentes non estis, si fratres vestros, quos indicando corrigere potestis, tacendo perire permittitis"). On Rebuke and Grace (426-427, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1513.htm) is a whole treatise against monks who said superiors should only pray for them and never rebuke them: "Let no one therefore say that a man must not be rebuked when he deviates from the right way" (chapter 25). Homily 7 on 1 John, section 8, the famous "Love, and do what you will", is about exactly this: "whether you correct, through love correct; whether you spare, through love do you spare". No change of mind on this point.

stances.summary: Every Christian must correct the people around them, even strangers in the street. Saying "that is none of my business" is a devilish answer, because we share one nature with every person.
stances.quote: And make me not this cold reply. What matters it to me? I have nothing in common with him. With the devil alone we have nothing in common, but with all men we have many things in common
stances.translation: W.R.W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9, 1889
stances.context: Preached at Antioch in 387. He asks his congregation to "correct on my behalf the blasphemers of this city", and in the same section goes further than any modern reader will expect: "should it be necessary to inflict blows, spare not to do so. Smite him on the face; strike his mouth; sanctify your hand with the blow". That line is genuine; handle it with care. Elsewhere he puts the gentle way first. Homily 60 on Matthew (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200160.htm) explains Matthew 18:15: tell the fault between the two of you alone, then with witnesses, and keep trying like a physician who does not give up on an obstinate illness. Homily 23 on Matthew (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200123.htm) insists that "Judge not" forbids bitter condemnation, not correction: "correct him, but not as a foe, nor as an adversary exacting a penalty, but as a physician providing medicines. For neither did Christ say, stay not him that is sinning, but judge not". Homilies 23 and 60 translated by George Prevost, revised by M.B. Riddle, NPNF 1st series vol. 10, 1888.

stances.summary: Keeping quiet about someone's sin is not kindness. The person who stays silent is the one without compassion, because he leaves the poison in the wound.
stances.quote: those who pretend to be kind (really suffering from the disease of men-pleasing) and fail to rebuke sinners, are actually sentencing them
stances.translation: W. K. L. Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (London: SPCK, 1925)
stances.location: Rule 72, section 6 (in Clarke's abbreviated translation of the Morals)
stances.context: The Morals are addressed to Christians generally; Clarke notes that rule 72 concerns "hearers", which "apparently means laity here". The full heading reads: "That we should accept blame and rebuke as a medicine removing disease and producing health. From which it is clear that those who pretend to be kind (really suffering from the disease of men-pleasing) and fail to rebuke sinners, are actually sentencing them and laying plots against their true life" (the OCR prints "lofe"). Morals 52.2 is simply "That one must not keep silence when men sin", and 51.1 adds "That a man must correct himself as regards every sin whatsoever before he accuses others." The rules for monks say the same. Shorter Rule 47 in Clarke (Rufinus 122), "Should we keep silence when men sin?", answers no and ends "what shall we say of those who know and remain silent? Grave is the danger of such". Shorter Rule 4 (Rufinus 17): "he who is silent lacks compassion, not he who rebukes; just as he who leaves the poison in him who is bitten by a venomous beast, not he that takes it out, is the merciless one". Longer Rule 46: every sin must be brought to the superior by those who know of it "if they cannot cure it themselves", because "to hide sin is to assist the sick man to his death". He also asks that rebuke be given "with the disposition of a father and doctor", never in anger. The OCR has small errors nearby ("1s" for "is"); the quote chosen avoids them.

stances.summary: If you see what is wrong in the people near you and say nothing, you are like a doctor who leaves a wound he could have healed. Silence is sometimes wise, but only for a while.
stances.quote: For those who take notice of what is evil in their neighbours, and yet refrain their tongue in silence, withdraw, as it were, the aid of medicine from observed sores, and become the causers of death, in that they would not cure the venom which they could have cured.
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series vol. 12, 1895
stances.location: Part 3, chapter 14 (Admonition 15: the over-silent and the talkative)
stances.context: Written c. 590. This chapter is advice a pastor gives to ordinary people who are "over-silent", so it applies to anyone, not only clergy. The same chapter keeps a place for silence: "The tongue, therefore, should be discreetly curbed, not tied up fast", and "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak". For pastors he is blunter (Part 2, chapter 4, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/36012.htm): silent pastors are the "Dumb dogs, that cannot bark" of Isaiah 56:10, and "for a shepherd to have feared to say what is right, what else is it but to have turned his back in keeping silence?" Part 2, chapter 10 adds the pastoral qualification: the vices of subjects "ought sometimes to be prudently connived at", or "seasonably tolerated" when there is no good moment to correct them, because "sores by being unseasonably cut are the worse enflamed".

stances.original: Neque dissimulet peccata delinquentium, sed mox, ut coeperint oriri, radicitus ea, ut praevalet, amputet: memor periculi Heli sacerdotis de Silo.
stances.summary: The one in charge must not look away from wrongdoing. He should deal with faults as soon as they appear, gently with the willing and more firmly with the stubborn.
stances.quote: Let him not shut his eyes to the faults of offenders; but as soon as they appear, let him strive with all his might to root them out,
stances.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 3rd ed. (Fort Augustus: Abbey Press, 1914)
stances.location: Chapter 2 (What kind of man the Abbot ought to be)
stances.context: Written c. 530-560. The sentence goes on: "remembering the fate of Heli, the priest of Silo" (Eli, who did not restrain his sons). This is addressed to the abbot. Chapter 23 sets the order for anyone at fault: "once or twice privately admonished by his elders. If he do not amend, let him be rebuked in public before all", then excommunication. Chapter 70 forbids ordinary monks to strike or excommunicate one another on their own authority, so correction runs through the elders and the abbot. Chapter 64 tempers it: "even in his corrections, let him act with prudence, and not go too far, lest while he seeketh too eagerly to scrape off the rust, the vessel be broken", adding "by this we do not mean that he should suffer vices to grow up".

stances.summary: When someone you love does something terribly wrong, you must tell him, even if he is the emperor and even if it costs you. Keeping quiet would bind your own conscience.
stances.quote: Should I keep silence? But then my conscience would be bound, my utterance taken away, which would be the most wretched condition of all.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, NPNF 2nd series vol. 10, 1896
stances.context: Written in 390 after Theodosius ordered the massacre at Thessalonica. Ambrose goes on to cite Ezekiel 3:18, tells the emperor he must do penance as David did, and says "I dare not offer the sacrifice if you intend to be present" (section 13). He confronts him privately first: "I am writing with my own hand that which you alone may read" (section 14), and says he preferred to raise the matter "privately... rather than possibly raise it by any action of mine in public" (section 5). Letter 40 (388) argues the same principle, that a priest must not keep silent before the emperor, but in defence of Christians who had burned a synagogue at Callinicum. Do not use that letter for the quiz; it will read today as defending a hate crime.

stances.summary: A sinner has every right, even a duty, to plead with another sinner to change. Being imperfect yourself is no excuse for keeping quiet.
stances.quote: If an apostle or a prophet, themselves immaculate, could speak thus with a clemency embracing all, how much more earnestly should a sinner like me plead with a sinner like you.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Date uncertain. The whole letter confronts a deacon over adultery at Rome and an attempt to seduce a nun at Bethlehem, and calls him to repent. Jerome also shows the cost of this habit. In Letter 117.1 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001117.htm) he at first refuses a request to rebuke a mother and daughter: "For through accusing crime I have been myself made out a criminal... Under the compulsion of an unhappy experience I have learned to be silent". Then he writes the rebuke anyway because the brother begs him. His letters are famous for their fierceness, so his side is clear in practice.

stances.summary: Telling someone off can be an act of friendship. An enemy scolds to mock you. A friend scolds because he cares.
stances.quote: Now censure is a mark of good-will, not of ill-will. For both he who is a friend and he who is not, reproach; but the enemy does so in scorn, the friend in kindness.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 190-200. Clement is defending the justice of God the Word, the divine Instructor, who both comforts and rebukes; the line about friends is a general principle he uses in that argument, so it is held but in passing. Chapter 9 lists the kinds of censure the Instructor uses and says "reproof and rebuke... are the stripes of the soul, chastizing sins, preventing death".

stances.summary: A person who sins openly should be corrected openly, and good people ought to welcome rebuke. But no one should judge another rashly.
stances.quote: That the sinner must be publicly reproved
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: Three Books of Testimonies against the Jews (To Quirinus)
stances.context: Written c. 248-250. The Testimonies are a handbook of Bible verses under headings Cyprian wrote himself; the heading is his, the proof text under it is 1 Timothy 5:20. Other headings in the same book: 102 "That all good men ought willingly to hear rebuke", 105 "That they are frequently to be corrected who do wrong in domestic duty", and, as a balance, 21 "That we must not rashly judge of another". Held clearly but only as a heading, hence strength 1.

stances.summary: The church is a place where wrongdoing is named. When Christians meet, they warn, rebuke and correct one another.
stances.quote: In the same place also exhortations are made, rebukes and sacred censures are administered.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 197, before his Montanist years. He is describing to pagans, with approval, what happens in the Christian assembly; it concerns the community's discipline rather than a private duty of one friend to another. The passage goes on to say that serious sinners are cut off "from us in prayer, in the congregation and in all sacred intercourse".

stances.summary: She told her famous brothers to their faces when they went wrong: Basil when he came home proud of his speaking, and Gregory when he complained about his troubles instead of giving thanks.
stances.quote: Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings? Will you not remedy the ingratitude of your soul?
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Life of St. Macrina (SPCK, 1916)
stances.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
stances.location: section on Gregory's last visit (Migne PG 46, col. 982A-B)
stances.context: Macrina's words as recorded by her brother Gregory of Nyssa, written c. 380-383 about her deathbed in 379. Gregory had just told her of his exile and the troubles of the Church; she answers with this rebuke and reminds him how much more he has than their parents had. Earlier in the Life Gregory tells how Basil came home from his studies "puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory" and "Macrina took him in hand" and drew him to the ascetic life. These are recorded deeds and one recorded speech, not a stated rule, hence strength 1.

stances.summary: He told a priest he had raised to his face that keeping horses and buying slaves was wrong. When the man turned on him, he forgave him and would not punish him.
stances.quote: For he had been reproved by him on the previous day, because he who had possessed nothing before he entered the clerical office, having, in fact, been brought up in the monastery by Martin himself, was now keeping horses and purchasing slaves.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Written c. 404 by Sulpicius, who knew Martin. Brictio (St Brice) had been raised in Martin's monastery. After this rebuke he stormed in and abused Martin, then came back and asked pardon. Martin would not remove him from the priesthood even when he was later accused of "many and great crimes", saying: "If Christ bore with Judas, why should not I bear with Brictio." Brictio later succeeded Martin as bishop of Tours. So Martin confronts the wrong but refuses to punish a man who had wronged him, "lest he should be suspected of revenging the injury done to himself". The line about the rebuke is Sulpicius's narration, not Martin's own words.

stances.summary: Hating no one does not mean saying nothing. Some people you must correct, some you pray for, and some you love more than your own life.
stances.quote: You shall not hate any man; but some you shall reprove, and concerning some you shall pray, and some you shall love more than your own life.
stances.translation: M.B. Riddle, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.work: The Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
stances.context: Anonymous church manual, late first or early second century. Chapter 15 adds: "reprove one another, not in anger, but in peace, as you have it in the Gospel". Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: We should accept correction without taking offence. Warning one another is good for us and draws us to God.
stances.quote: Let us receive correction, beloved, on account of which no one should feel displeased. Those exhortations by which we admonish one another are both good [in themselves], and highly profitable, for they tend to unite us to the will of God.
stances.translation: John Keith, ANF vol. 9, 1896
stances.work: First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Clement)
stances.context: Written c. 96 from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth, which had deposed its elders. The whole letter is itself a long, courteous rebuke. The chapter title "Let Us Admonish and Correct One Another" is the translator's, not Clement's. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Loving your family does not excuse you from warning them. God is angry with a father who let his children go wrong without a word.
stances.quote: And although you love your sons, yet did you not warn your house, but permitted them to be terribly corrupted. On this account is the Lord angry with you
stances.translation: F. Crombie, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Rome, first half of the second century. The words are spoken to Hermas by the woman of his vision (the Church); she goes on: "Cease not therefore to admonish your sons". A family setting, which may suit a plain quiz statement. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: When a respected member of the church goes wrong, do not treat him as an enemy, but do call him back.
stances.quote: but call them back as suffering and straying members, that you may save your whole body.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Early second century. The case is Valens, a former presbyter at Philippi who had fallen into greed. Polycarp grieves for him and his wife, and just before this line asks the church to "be then moderate in regard to this matter, and do not count such as enemies". Gentle correction, not silence. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.original: Latin systematic collection (Verba Seniorum 9.4, PL 73, OCR at archive.org/download/patrologiaecur73mign): "Peccata mea sunt post me currentia, et non video ea, et veni ego hodie judicare aliena peccata?"
stances.summary: I have enough sins of my own running out behind me. Who am I to sit in judgement on my brother?
stances.quote: And he said unto them, "[The sands are] my sins " which are running down behind me and I cannot see them, "and I, even I, have come this day to judge shortcomings
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (London: Chatto & Windus, 1907), translated from the Syriac of Anan-Isho
stances.work: The Sayings of the Holy Fathers (Paradise, vol. 2), chapter Of Humility
stances.context: A brother at Scetis had done wrong and a council met to judge him. Moses refused to come, then arrived carrying "a basket with a hole in it" filled with sand. The quotation stops at a page turn in the scan; the next words are "which are not mine", and "when they heard [this] they set free that brother and said nothing [further] to him." The Latin version has an old basket of sand; the popular retelling from the Greek alphabetical collection (Moses 2) has a leaking jug of water. Both are genuine versions of one story. The setting is a public judgement, not one friend quietly speaking to another. Budge also gives "the words which Abba Moses said to Abba Poemen" (sayings 119-120): "It is better for a man to put himself to death rather than his neighbour, and he should not condemn him in anything." The Sayings call him simply Abba Moses of Scetis; tradition identifies him with Moses the Ethiopian (Moses the Black), d. c. 405. Cassian's Abba Moses of Conferences 1-2 may be the same man; that is disputed.

stances.summary: If I happened to see a brother sinning as I passed by, I would walk on as if I had not seen. Hate your own sins and make excuses for your neighbour's.
stances.quote: Some of the old men asked Abba Poemen, saying, "If "we see one of the brethren committing sin, wouldst thou "have us rebuke him?" And the old man said unto them, " If I had some business which made me pass by him, and in " passing by him I saw him committing sin, I should pass him " by and not see him."
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (London: Chatto & Windus, 1907), translated from the Syriac of Anan-Isho
stances.work: The Sayings of the Holy Fathers (Paradise, vol. 2), chapter Of Scrupulous Watchfulness in our Thoughts and Words and Deeds
stances.context: Fifth-century Egypt. The question put to him is almost exactly the quiz claim. He says it again and again in Budge: "The hatred of evil things is for a man to hate his own sins, and to justify those of his neighbour" (541); "No monk should condemn any man in anything" (456); asked whether he should give commands to brothers living with him: "No, be unto them an example, and not a lawgiver" (457). Saying 286 follows with a story of a monk who kicked what he thought was a couple sinning and found sacks of wheat: "unless ye have felt with your hands ye should not offer rebuke." In the Latin systematic collection (Verba Seniorum 9.5-9.6, PL 73) Poemen also answers the question "Si videro culpam fratris mei, bonum est celare eam?" with "Quacunque hora tegimus peccatum fratris nostri, teget etiam Deus nostrum" (whenever we cover our brother's sin, God will cover ours); Budge gives that saying to an unnamed old man (Questions and Answers 358). He did allow a gentle word that avoids accusation (608): "If a man sinneth, and he saith, 'I have not sinned,' and thou chidest him, thou cuttest off his will; but if thou sayest unto him, 'Be not sorry about this, but guard thyself from sinning again,' by these means thou wakest his soul to repentance." The stray quotation marks at line starts in the quote are printed as in the scan.

stances.summary: Do not scold anyone or try to put them right, even very bad people. Throw your cloak over the sinner and cover him, and bear shame yourself rather than expose him.
stances.quote: Do not vituperate any one and do not direct any one, not even those who are very evil in their behaviour. Spread thy mantle over the sinner and cover him,
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, 1923), from the Syriac; public domain
stances.work: Mystic Treatises, Treatise 50, "Short sections containing various considerations in which is shown the injury caused by foolish zeal under the pretext of fear of God and the profit originating in quietness"
stances.context: Late seventh century; bishop of Nineveh in the Church of the East, outside the imperial Church but honoured as a saint by the Orthodox. The passage continues: "If thou art not able to take upon thee his transgressions and to receive chastisement in his stead, at least suffer exposure, in order not to expose him... Do not love to be a judge. Thou must know, o my brother, that we stay indoors in order not to know the evil deeds of men." So it is advice to solitaries first of all. The same treatise opens (p. 230): "those who are sick, are in want of nursing more than in want of vituperation", yet also says "direct the transgressor in a meek spirit" (Galatians 6:1). Treatise 45 (pp. 215-216) allows a private, loving word: "He that cures his brother privately gives a proof of the strength of his love, but he who exposes him in the presence of his comrades betrays the force of his envy." In the treatise "On those who live in the neighbourhood" (p. 273): "Why doest thou rebuke the sinner, o man?" His thrust is against zeal to correct, with room for quiet, gentle healing. The OCR has errors nearby ("chastiscment", "expo- sure"); the quote avoids them.

stances.summary: He covered up the faults he saw as if he had not seen them. God sees the sinner and is patient, so who am I to rebuke him?
stances.quote: They used to tell a story about Abba Macarius the Great, who became, as it is written, an earthly God, for as God overshadoweth the world so also did Abba Macarius cover over the shortcomings which he saw as if he did not see them, and the things which he heard as if he heard them not.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (London: Chatto & Windus, 1907), translated from the Syriac of Anan-Isho
stances.work: Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men (Paradise, vol. 2)
stances.context: Macarius of Egypt, d. c. 390. The next saying (245) tells how he saw a brother sinning with a woman at night "but he did not rebuke him", and said: "If God Who fashioned him seeth [him], and is long-suffering, for if He so desired He could consume him, who am I that I should rebuke him?" (that line is broken by a page turn in the scan). Stories told about him by others, hence strength 1. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: When a sinner was thrown out of church, he walked out with him. If one sin makes a man unfit, I with my many sins am less fit still.
stances.quote: and there was there a man of discretion whose name was Bessarion, and he also arose and went out of the church, and said, “ If ye have judged that “ this man who hath committed only one offence is not fit to “ worship God, how very much less fit am I, who have com- “ mitted many sins, to do so?”
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (London: Chatto & Windus, 1907), translated from the Syriac of Anan-Isho
stances.work: The Sayings of the Holy Fathers (Paradise, vol. 2), chapter Of Humility
stances.context: Fourth-century Egypt. This is about public expulsion by a priest rather than a private word of correction. The Latin systematic collection (Verba Seniorum 9.2, PL 73) has the short form: "Et ego peccator sum" (I too am a sinner). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Do not go looking for other people's faults or talk about them. You are not the judge. If you love what is right, correct yourself.
stances.quote: Search not out the faults of men; reveal not the sin of your fellow; the shortcomings of your neighbours, in speech of the mouth repeat not. You are not judge in creation, you have not dominion over the earth. If you love righteousness, reprove your soul and yourself. Be judge unto your own sins, and chastener of your own transgressions.
stances.translation: A. Edward Johnston, NPNF 2nd series vol. 13, 1898
stances.context: The next section (13) adds: "Him that sins blame not, lest you also be put to confusion. To him that repents of his sins be a helper and counsellor". Section 3 implies that a loving rebuke is possible: "If in envy you rebuke, wicked is all your reproof." Caution: this homily is printed under Ephrem's name from a Syriac collection, and many sermons under his name are later imitations; I did not confirm that scholars accept this one as genuine. Use it only with that caution.

stances.summary: People need different medicine. Some need a public rebuke, some a private one, and with some it is better to see nothing and say nothing, so as not to crush them.
stances.quote: Of others it is better to take no notice, but seeing not to see, and hearing not to hear them, according to the proverb, that we may not drive them to despair, under the depressing influence of repeated reproofs
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight to Pontus)
stances.context: Written c. 362 about the pastor's task. Section 31 gives the other half: "Some are benefited by praise, others by blame... some are set right by encouragement, others by rebuke; some, when taken to task in public, others, when privately corrected." A deliberate middle view: correction is a medicine to be dosed, and sometimes the right dose is none. Written about pastors.

stances.summary: Harsh rebuke can drive a struggling person to despair. Meet weakness with sympathy and gentle comfort, not severe words.
stances.quote: And so learn from your own experience to sympathize with those in trouble, and never to terrify with destructive despair those who are in danger, nor harden them with severe speeches, but rather restore them with gentle and kindly consolations
stances.translation: C.S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Written c. 426. The words are Abba Apollos's, told by Abba Moses and written down by Cassian. An old monk had attacked a young monk who confessed his temptations "with the bitterest reproaches" and nearly drove him out of the monastic life; Apollos prays that the same temptation fall on the old man so that he learns sympathy. Cassian tells the story "without giving the name of the actor, lest we might be guilty of something of the same kind as the man who published abroad the sins of the brother". But he is no enemy of correction: Institutes 4.16 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/350704.htm) describes, with approval, Egyptian monasteries where even breaking a jar or coming late to prayer is corrected publicly. His point is how to correct, not whether.

stances.summary: Shield a sinner from public exposure, then speak one quiet word to him alone.
stances.quote: and finally he took the brother by the hand, and said unto him, " Take heed to thy soul, O my brother," and having said this he departed, and he refused to make public the matter of the brother.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (London: Chatto & Windus, 1907), translated from the Syriac of Anan-Isho
stances.work: The Sayings of the Holy Fathers (Paradise, vol. 2), chapter Of Love, and Charity, and of the Welcoming of Strangers
stances.context: Fourth century; Budge calls him "the blessed Bishop Ammon" (Ammonas, disciple of Antony). A crowd came to expel a brother who had a woman in his cell; the brother hid her under a large earthenware vessel, and Ammon, "understanding what that brother had done, for the sake of God hid the matter. And he went in and sat upon the earthenware vessel". He rebuked the crowd ("May God forgive you"), then gave the brother this private warning. Not in the candidate pool.

splits_fathers: Real voices exist on both sides, and the split is clean. Most bishops, preachers and rule-writers, East and West, from the Didache on, say that correcting a wrongdoer is a duty of love and that silence is itself a sin: Augustine (the strongest and most repeated), John Chrysostom, Basil, Gregory the Great, Benedict, Ambrose and Jerome, with lighter support from Clement of Alexandria, Cyprian, Tertullian, Clement of Rome, Hermas and Polycarp; Macrina and Martin did it in practice. Almost all of them add conditions: in love, privately first, at the right moment, correcting yourself first (Basil, Morals 51.1), never in anger. The strongest voices against are the Egyptian desert elders and the Syriac ascetic tradition: Moses the Black (the leaking basket), Poemen ("I should pass him by and not see him"), Macarius, Bessarion and Isaac the Syrian ("Spread thy mantle over the sinner and cover him"), with the homily printed under Ephrem's name. They mostly speak to monks about their own humility and about public councils that judge a brother, and several still allow one quiet, gentle word (Poemen 608, Ammonas, Isaac Treatise 45). In the middle: Gregory of Nazianzus (sometimes "seeing not to see") and Cassian (never harshly). So it maps roughly onto pastor or rule-giver against desert elder. It is not East against West: Basil and Chrysostom are Greek and on the duty side.
splits_people_today: Genuinely divided, which makes it a good quiz item. Many people today, Christian or not, lean to "who am I to judge" and "mind your own business", especially about private matters such as sex, drinking, money or religion, and especially younger people. Barna's 2007 study unChristian reported that 87 percent of young non-Christian Americans described Christians as judgmental, and Pope Francis's "Who am I to judge?" (2013) is widely quoted with approval. Others hold that real friends speak up ("friends don't let friends drive drunk", family interventions, speaking up at work), and many churchgoers know Matthew 18:15 and would agree. Expect churchgoers, especially evangelicals and traditional Catholics, to lean agree, and the unaffiliated and many mainline Christians to lean disagree. Most people's answer turns on two things the statement leaves open: how close they are to the person, and whether the wrong harms someone else. The word "duty" will push some people who would speak up anyway towards "disagree".

misattributions.line: Love the sinner, hate the sin
misattributions.truth: Not his wording. The nearest real line is in his Rule (Letter 211.11 in its form for women): "with due love for the persons and hatred of the sin" (Latin Rule: "cum dilectione hominum et odio vitiorum"). It closes the passage about watching, reporting and punishing a sister's faults, so it is a line about how to correct people, not about leaving them alone. The short proverb form is best known from Gandhi's Autobiography: "Hate the sin and not the sinner".

misattributions.line: Love, and do what you will
misattributions.truth: Genuine (Homily 7 on 1 John, section 8), but usually quoted as a licence to do as you please. In context it is about correction: a father who beats his son out of love against a kidnapper who caresses; "whether you correct, through love correct; whether you spare, through love do you spare".

misattributions.line: If we cover our brother's sin, God will cover ours
misattributions.truth: Not a fake, but the attribution depends on the collection. The Latin systematic collection (Verba Seniorum 9.5-9.6, PL 73) gives it to Poemen; Budge's translation of the Syriac (Questions and Answers 358) gives it to an unnamed old man.

misattributions.line: Moses the Black carried a leaking jug of water
misattributions.truth: Genuine in the Greek alphabetical collection (Moses 2), but Budge's Syriac and the Latin systematic collection have a leaky basket of sand. A different elder, Pior, carried a sack of sand on his back and a small bag of it in front (Verba Seniorum 9.9), and the two stories are sometimes merged. Pick one version and cite it.

notes: Best pair for the reveal: Augustine, City of God 1.9 or Sermon 82 ("You are worse in keeping silence, than he in his reviling"), against Poemen saying 285 ("I should pass him by and not see him") or Moses's basket of sand. Chrysostom's Homily 1 on the Statues is a vivid agree voice, but in the same breath he tells people to hit blasphemers in the face; do not quote the milder line without knowing that. Do not use Ambrose's Letter 40 (the Callinicum synagogue) for this question. Many duty voices speak to superiors (Benedict chapter 2, Gregory Pastoral Rule 2.4, Basil Longer Rule 46); the ones that plainly address ordinary people are Augustine City of God 1.9, Gregory Pastoral Rule 3.14, Basil Morals 72.6, Chrysostom Statues 1.32, the Didache and Hermas. Budge quotations are copied from archive.org OCR and keep its stray quotation marks at line starts; clean them for display. Leads I did not confirm, and why: John Climacus, Ladder step 10 on judging (no English before 1929, and I could not load the Greek); Dorotheus of Gaza, Discourse 6 on not judging (modern English only; not loaded); Hilary's "it is time to speak" (Against Constantius 1; not found in the OCR of PL 10); Origen, Commentary on Matthew 13.30 (explains Matthew 18:15 without a clear stance of his own); Antony's shipwreck parable (Verba Seniorum 9.1) is about taking back an expelled brother, so it belongs with second chances; Agathon's "Do not commit the thing thyself" (Budge 356) is about not judging in thought, and the OCR garbles it; Arsenius's "That I have spoken I have many times repented; that I held my peace I have never repented" (Budge 549) is about speech in general, not correcting others. I found nothing on this question for Syncletica, Evagrius, Pelagius, Lactantius, Justin, Irenaeus, Ignatius, Hippolytus, Novatian, Perpetua, Athanasius, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa (except as Macrina's narrator), Paulinus or Boethius.
